analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicaid drug manufacturer rebates to managed care plans serving Medicaid enrollees.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 2009 with 10 Senate Democrats behind it, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a committee vote, floor vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicaid, states get mandatory rebates from drug manufacturers when drugs are dispensed through traditional fee-for-service Medicaid, but people enrolled in private Medicaid managed care plans have not benefited from those rebates because the plans have historically been exempt. This bill would require managed care plans' contracts to make their covered drugs subject to the same manufacturer rebates the state gets, and would require the plans' payment rates to reflect the actual rebate savings. It would also require states to report rebate amounts quarterly and make aggregate data public.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid enrollees in managed care plans, whose drug coverage would be backed by the same manufacturer discounts as traditional Medicaid, along with state budgets and taxpayers, who bear a large share of Medicaid drug costs. States could use the rebate savings to fund coverage or hold down costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income Medicaid enrollees and state budgets

how_it_helps.text: Requires that payment for drugs dispensed to Medicaid managed care enrollees be subject to the same manufacturer rebate the state is subject to under the fee-for-service rebate agreement.

Requires capitation rates paid to managed care plans to be based on actual cost experience related to rebates and to meet federal actuarially-sound-rate rules, so rebate savings flow back rather than being absorbed.

Requires states to report quarterly to the Secretary the total dollar amount and volume of rebates received for both brand-name and generic drugs, and requires the Secretary to make the aggregate data publicly available after review.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would owe rebates on drugs dispensed through Medicaid managed care plans that they currently do not pay because of the managed care exemption. Medicaid managed care insurers would collect and pass through the rebates, with their payment rates adjusted to match actual rebate experience.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets managed care plans restrict coverage of drugs using their own formulary, utilization management, and cost-sharing policies, with state approval of the formulary, so some enrollees could face narrower drug access even as prices fall.
Plans may run 'positive' formulary lists that exclude drugs unless patients get them through prior authorization, which can add delays and paperwork for enrollees and their doctors.

Tying manufacturer rebates more tightly into Medicaid could give manufacturers added reason to raise list prices, since rebate obligations are calculated from them; this dynamic already exists in fee-for-service Medicaid and would extend to managed care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: managed care enrollees and state budgets gain manufacturer discounts that traditional Medicaid already gets, at the cost of payments from brand-name drug makers and somewhat more plan discretion over which drugs are covered. The bill tries to limit abuse of that discretion by keeping state approval over formularies and requiring public reporting of rebate data, but prior authorization hurdles for excluded drugs would be a genuine burden for some patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it died in committee without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman introduced the Drug Rebate Equalization Act of 2009 in the Senate on March 9, 2009, joined by Senators Casey, Stabenow, and Whitehouse as original sponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on March 9, 2009.
No further action was ever taken on the bill — no committee markup, no report, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
Nine additional Democratic senators cosponsored the bill during the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, so they continued to avoid paying Medicaid rebates on drugs dispensed through managed care plans, and Congress later enacted a health law that kept that exemption in place.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for extending Medicaid fee-for-service rebates to managed care enrollees.

for.name: 9 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding to the four original Democratic sponsors.

against.name: Chair, Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it received no markup, report, or vote after referral.

against.name: PhRMA and brand-name drug manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Medicaid rebates to managed care, and industry negotiations during the 2009-2010 health debate succeeded in preserving the managed care rebate exemption in the law that Congress enacted instead.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters were Democrats and no floor vote ever occurred, so the bill never produced a recorded partisan split.

industries.note: They currently avoid the Medicaid rebate on drugs dispensed through managed care plans; the bill would make them pay the same rebates as in fee-for-service Medicaid. Their gain from the bill dying is a cost borne by state budgets and Medicaid enrollees.

The bill keeps these plans as the delivery channel for Medicaid drug coverage and even expands their flexibility to set formularies and manage utilization, while requiring their rates to reflect actual rebate savings. They keep their gatekeeper role and revenue, with rebates passed through rather than absorbed.
